content: The analysis demonstrates the positioning of various algorithms when comparing Health Adjusted Life Years (HALYs), which combine mortality and morbidity, against discounted costs. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) reached the following conclusions when comparing HPV testing to VIA or cytology testing: 1. Primary HPV testing without triage was found to be on the cost-effectiveness frontier: Testing every 10 years at ages 35–45 resulted in an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $154 per HALY saved. Testing every 10 years at ages 30–50 resulted in an ICER of $393 per HALY saved. Testing every 5 years at ages 30–50 resulted in an ICER of $502 per HALY saved. 2. Primary HPV testing with HPV 16/18 genotyping for triage had similar costs and effects, suggesting comparable cost-effectiveness outcomes. 3. As a reference for willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds, the population-weighted average GDP per capita for 2019 across 78 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) was $1,999. Additionally, 87% of these countries (68 out of 78) had a GDP per capita greater than $500. 4. The findings were robust even under assumptions of lower compliance. The GDG noted that the costs of HPV testing alone and HPV testing with HPV 16/18 triage were similar. This was attributed to a higher number of treatments with HPV testing alone but fewer treatments with HPV 16/18 triage, which incurred additional testing costs. Equity Considerations The GDG agreed that providing HPV DNA testing could potentially increase access to screening, although no direct evidence was available to confirm this. Acceptability A survey of GDG members revealed moderate to high concern regarding the financial sustainability of scaling up all algorithms (cytology > HPV > VIA). There was also significant concern about minimizing patient costs for HPV and cytology algorithms. A separate survey of 561 women conducted anonymously online in 2020 found: 56% of women reported no barriers to attending a screening program. 78% expressed a strong preference for immediate treatment following a diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial lesions. Follow-up visits after treatment were perceived as challenging. There was aversion to the use of a speculum during screening. The community requested better counseling, patient education, and availability of treatment and screening test options. A systematic review of 43 qualitative studies showed high acceptability (70% or higher, with several studies reporting over 90%) for self-sampling, VIA, HPV DNA tests, or triage-based methods. Women generally preferred to make their own decisions about treatment, with few consulting their partners or feeling obligated to do so. Factors reducing acceptability included lack of reminders, test costs, low education levels, absence of children, recent HIV diagnosis, poor awareness of cervical cancer, and inadequate provider-patient relationships. Feasibility A survey of GDG members highlighted concerns about the feasibility of implementing screening algorithms: Over 70% were moderately to very concerned about generating demand for screening across all algorithms, with the highest concern for VIA (~80%). Access to HPV or cytology screening was a greater concern (30–40%) compared to VIA. Maintaining a trained workforce for VIA and cytology was a significant concern (~90%) compared to HPV (~55%). Infrastructure demands for HPV or cytology were moderately or very concerning for over 50% of respondents. Maintaining registries (aggregate or patient-level) was a concern for all algorithms (>75%). Integration with other programs raised variable concerns, with cytology > HPV > VIA. The GDG also noted: Complex algorithms may be challenging to implement. Multiple steps across health sectors could reduce feasibility. Political will and sustaining a skilled workforce are critical factors. Summary of Judgments Desirable effects: Moderate to large. Undesirable effects: Trivial to small. Certainty of evidence: Moderate. Cost-effectiveness: Likely favors HPV DNA testing. Equity: Likely increased. Acceptability: High. Feasibility: Moderate to high. Recommendations 1. Existing programs using quality-assured cytology as the primary screening test should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational. Programs using VIA should transition rapidly due to quality assurance challenges. 2. WHO suggests using HPV DNA testing as the primary screening test, with or without triage, to prevent cervical cancer in the general population of women. 3. In a screen-and-treat approach using HPV DNA detection, women testing positive for HPV DNA should be treated. 4. In a screen, triage, and treat approach, triage options such as partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology may be used after a positive HPV DNA test. The choice of triage method should depend on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and resources. Screening Intervals WHO suggests regular screening intervals of 5–10 years when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test. This recommendation is based on modeled evidence showing greater benefits and fewer harms with these intervals compared to more frequent screening or similar intervals using cytology or VIA. Women Living with HIV Primary HPV testing every 3 or 5 years resulted in the largest reductions in cervical cancer incidence. Testing every 5 years for ages 25–50 reduced cervical cancer incidence by over 62%, while testing every 3 years reduced it by over 67%. Primary VIA testing every 3 years had a lower impact on cervical cancer incidence compared to HPV testing every 5 years.
